content:
We’re excited to announce several major improvements to LeanSearch:

  1. Upgraded to Lean & mathlib v4.24.
  2. A new search engine built by @Guoxiong Gao , with notably better retrieval for definitions and structures, without sacrificing performance on theorems and instances, with a slightly higher computational cost on the server end.
  3. Items from Std and Lean are now fully and correctly indexed; Fields of structures and constructors of inductive types are now also indexed.
  4. Other small fixes and quality-of-life improvements across the UI/UX.
    Give it a try and let us know what you think!

Hi everyone! We've rolled out a major update to leansearch.net, including a new retrieval engine and expanded server capacity. We've also written up the full technical evolution of LeanSearch since the original paper (A Semantic Search Engine for Mathlib4, Gao et al. 2024):

LeanSearch v2: Global Premise Retrieval for Lean 4 Theorem Proving
arXiv:2605.13137 | Code & data | Pre-built corpus: cuVS / JSONL

The paper describes two modes. Standard mode is the upgraded single-query retrieval pipeline (hierarchy-aware informalization, Qwen3-Embedding / Qwen3-Reranker, cuVS CAGRA indexing, etc.) that powers leansearch.net today, achieving state-of-the-art nDCG@10 on our benchmark without domain-specific fine-tuning. Reasoning mode is the main academic contribution: an iterative sketch-retrieve-reflect loop targeting global premise retrieval (recovering the full set of library lemmas a theorem's proof requires), which recovers 46.1% of ground-truth premise groups within 10 candidates. Reasoning mode is not yet available as a public API due to LLM cost, but all code, data, and prompts are fully open-sourced for local reproduction.

A note on timing: these improvements were made incrementally over the past two years; we simply wrote them up together. Most standard-mode upgrades have been live on leansearch.net since March. We will continue to ship improvements as soon as they're ready, not waiting for papers.

Service updates

Engine. leansearch.net now runs our latest standard-mode pipeline. The API remains open as always. Docs: <https://leansearch.net/docs>. API response time is typically ~0.2 s (faster than the web GUI).

Mathlib version. The backend currently indexes Mathlib v4.28.0-rc1. We are working on updating to the latest Mathlib (this requires updating jixia) and expect to ship it soon.

Stats page. We've added a usage dashboard at <https://leansearch.net/stats.html>.

Usage growth. Since roughly January 2026, coinciding with the wave of coding agents (Claude Code, OpenClaw, etc.) writing Lean, usage has grown sharply. LeanSearch has now served over 6 million cumulative requests, with nearly 1 million in the past week alone. We welcome both agent and human traffic and will do our best to support it.

Privacy policy. Given the increasing load, we need a better picture of per-user request patterns to manage capacity. Until now we did not store IPs, so we are updating our privacy policy to begin logging them for this purpose.

Capacity and rate limits. Over the past two months, server capacity was ~8 req/s with a per-IP limit of 60 req/min. We noticed the lean-lsp-mcp project sets its LeanSearch rate to 3 requests per 30 seconds; we'd encourage setting this higher. Recently the server has been hitting its ceiling, causing some requests to go unserved and affecting the experience for users on the web GUI. As of today, we have further optimized the backend and added compute: capacity is now ~40 req/s and the per-IP limit is raised to 120 req/min. We will monitor server load and dynamically adjust the per-IP rate limit, increasing it as capacity allows while ensuring that individual users on the web GUI are not affected.

LeanSearch has been publicly available for two years now. The support from the Lean community has been far more than we ever expected, and it is heartwarming to see usage grow alongside the community itself, from a modest number of human users to an ecosystem where both people and agents rely on it daily. Your encouragement is what drives us to keep improving LeanSearch, and it is what made this paper possible. LeanSearch will remain fully open-source, and we look forward to continuing to grow alongside this community. Thank you all for making LeanSearch what it is today.

Due to the ongoing migration of our deployed GPU computing cluster, leansearch.net is expected to be offline for approximately 2–3 days. We will complete the cluster migration as quickly as possible and bring the service back online once it is ready.
The cluster migration has been completed, and leansearch.net is now back online and running normally. Thank you all for your patience and understanding!
Do you have plans for making reasoning mode more publicly available? It sounds like a neat advancement
